children: By Beckie Strum
Anthropic's lower-than-expected valuation, between $1 trillion and $1.4 trillion, still spells an incredible windfall for its workforce.

The Claude creator, which employs about 5,300 people, is forging ahead with an initial public offering that will shower an unprecedented amount of wealth on its own staff, who will have to navigate the unique challenges of becoming multimillionaires overnight.

Columbia Business School Professor Shivaram Rajgopal offered some back-of-the-envelope calculations based on Anthropic's IPO filing. Altogether, employee stock options, restricted stock units (RSUs), and the co-founders' combined stake totals about 27% to 32% of the company, Rajgopal estimated.
"So conservatively, at least a fourth of the company is with employees, including founders, which is amazing — like a huge, huge number," Rajgopal said.

Anthropic expects an IPO price of $70 to $78 a share this coming Wednesday, with Nasdaq trading to follow the next day. Even at the low end, employee stock options would be worth more than $100 billion, according to the filing. That pencils out to $20 million per employee, though of course stock options aren't evenly distributed. Meanwhile, the Bloomberg Billionaires Index estimates each of the company's seven co-founders to be worth $18 billion.
Each of the co-founders is selling about $250 million worth of Class A stock in the IPO, while CFO Krishna Rao will sell shares equal to about $700,000, according to the filing.
"Of course, there are all kinds of caveats," Rajgopal said. "There'll be some taxes and there'll be lockup periods, and this and that. But still, the headline number is big."

A concern that has already emerged among the company's newly minted millionaires is security. "One thing that's very notable is the desire for privacy," said San Francisco-based Nina Hatvany, a luxury real estate agent with Compass. "They just really, really don't want people to know where they live."

Hatvany has helped Anthropic and OpenAI employees, all in their 20s and 30s with hefty budgets, find homes in San Francisco's prime neighborhoods. They insist on nondisclosure agreements and purchase property via limited liability companies to shield their identities in public records, she said.

An obsession with security goes right up to Anthropic's top brass. Compared with S&P 500 tech and software executives, CEO Dario Amodei falls in the bottom third when it comes to compensation (he made $18 million in 2025, according to the IPO filing). But he rises to the top 4% in terms of security spending, according to an analysis by Equilar, a data firm that focuses on executive compensation.
Anthropic paid $2.84 million on personal security for Amodei in 2025, including nearly $100,000 for private air travel, according to the IPO filing.

But Anthropic's workforce is young and inexperienced, and the desire for anonymity in public property records has met a learning curve. "There's a little bit of education around how these things work," Hatvany said. "I caution them, you know, they mustn't sign anything."

In the context of IPO windfalls, Anthropic employees are also likely to put a greater emphasis on philanthropy given the company's culture and unorthodox setup as a public-benefit corporation. Each of the seven co-founders have pledged to give 80% of their personal company equity to charity, according to the IPO filing, which also outlined a generous company-matching program for employees who donate stock.

Besides homes and giving, the fresh batch of ultrarich will likely find themselves preoccupied with much duller tasks to start. The biggest will be sorting out how much of their newfound wealth goes to Uncle Sam and when.

"There is always, or often, a tax drag associated with getting wealth," said Bob Petix, a private wealth strategist at Wells Fargo. The worst mistake would be "not taking into account the tax that's associated with this. You you cannot look at the gross number. It almost has no meaning. That's number one."
Some of these 20- and 30-year-olds will be presented with a whole alphabet soup of inheritance and tax strategies they have never had to think about before.
"Simple 'I love you' wills will not suffice," Petix said.

That is why private banks and wealth managers have descended on the company. They are eager to turn Anthropic employees into clients and are jockeying for a place on the company's vetted list of firms, Financial News reported earlier this week.

"For some individuals, it's going to be life-changing, but it's not going to have that same intergenerational implication," Petix said. "For those who it may, they're not thinking in those terms because they're not largely from long-term wealth. It involves a whole new set of ideas and thinking that you need to get your head around."
